Autoimmune describes anything related to a situation where your own body's defense system turns against your own body.
Start here: What your immune system normally does

Your body has a powerful internal security force called the immune system. Its job is to detect and destroy things that don't belong — bacteria, viruses, parasites, fungi, cancerous cells. To do this job, it needs to tell the difference between two kinds of things:

  • "Self" — your own healthy cells and tissues. Leave these alone.
  • "Non-self" — foreign invaders. Attack and destroy these.

This distinction is absolutely critical. A healthy immune system is like a well-trained guard who knows exactly who belongs in the building and who is an intruder.
What goes wrong in an autoimmune situation

In an autoimmune situation, this recognition system breaks down. The immune system misidentifies your own healthy cells as enemies and launches an attack against them — as if your own tissues were dangerous foreign invaders.

Think of it this way: the guard loses his list, gets confused, and starts attacking the very employees he was supposed to protect.

The word autoimmune is built around this idea. "Auto" means "self." So autoimmune literally signals: the immune system acting against the self.
How the adjective is used

You'll almost always see "autoimmune" placed in front of a noun to describe something connected to this misfiring process:

  • Autoimmune disease / autoimmune disorder / autoimmune condition — a disease caused by the immune system attacking the body's own tissues. This is the most common use of the word.
  • Autoimmune response — the specific act of the immune system attacking self-tissue.
  • Autoimmune attack — the episode or flare during which this attack occurs.
  • Autoimmune marker — a measurable sign in blood tests that suggests the immune system is targeting self-tissue.
What an autoimmune disease actually looks like

When the immune system attacks healthy tissue, it causes inflammation and damage in that specific area. What the disease feels like depends entirely on which part of the body is being attacked.

Here are some well-known autoimmune diseases, along with what the immune system is wrongly targeting in each:

  • Type 1 Diabetes — the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas are attacked. Result: the body can't produce insulin, so blood sugar goes unregulated.
  • Rheumatoid Arthritis — the lining of the joints is attacked. Result: painful, swollen, stiff joints, often in the hands and feet.
  • Lupus (SLE) — the immune system attacks multiple organs — the skin, kidneys, heart, brain, and joints. Result: a wide range of symptoms across the body, including rashes, fatigue, and organ damage.
  • Multiple Sclerosis (MS) — the protective coating (myelin) around nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord is attacked. Result: disrupted nerve signals, causing problems with movement, vision, balance, and more.
  • Hashimoto's Thyroiditis — the thyroid gland is attacked. Result: an underactive thyroid, causing fatigue, weight gain, and slowed metabolism.
  • Psoriasis — skin cells are targeted. Result: the skin produces cells too rapidly, forming thick, scaly patches.
  • Celiac Disease — the lining of the small intestine is attacked when gluten (a protein in wheat, barley, rye) is consumed. Result: damaged intestinal lining, poor nutrient absorption.

Each of these is called an autoimmune disease because the root cause is the same in all: the immune system fighting the body itself.
The weapon the immune system misuses: autoantibodies

Normally, your immune system makes proteins called antibodies to tag foreign invaders for destruction. In autoimmune conditions, the immune system makes a particular type of antibody called an autoantibody — an antibody directed against your own tissues. Detecting autoantibodies in a blood test is one of the key ways doctors confirm that a disease is autoimmune in nature.
Why does this happen?

The exact cause varies, but the leading factors are:

  1. Genetics — some people inherit genes that make their immune system more likely to misfire. Autoimmune diseases can run in families.
  2. Environmental triggers — certain infections, chemicals, or exposures may trigger the immune misfiring in genetically susceptible people.
  3. Sex hormones — women are significantly more likely to develop autoimmune diseases than men, suggesting hormones play a role.
  4. A disrupted gut microbiome — the community of microorganisms in the digestive tract appears to influence how the immune system learns to distinguish self from non-self.

Often, it's a combination of genetic susceptibility plus a trigger — not a single cause.
Autoimmune vs. allergy: an important distinction

Both involve the immune system reacting when it shouldn't, but they're different:

  • In an allergy, the immune system overreacts to something outside the body that is harmless — like pollen, dust, or peanuts.
  • In an autoimmune condition, the immune system attacks something inside the body — your own cells and tissues.

The target is different. Allergies target external substances; autoimmune conditions target the self.
Is autoimmune disease curable?

In most cases, no — not yet. Autoimmune diseases are typically chronic (long-lasting or lifelong) conditions. However, they are often manageable. Treatment usually aims to:

  • Suppress the overactive immune response (using immunosuppressant drugs)
  • Reduce inflammation and tissue damage
  • Manage symptoms and prevent flares (episodes when the disease worsens)

The challenge in treatment is that suppressing the immune system to stop the attack also makes the person more vulnerable to real infections. So doctors constantly balance between calming the immune system enough to prevent self-attack, without leaving the person unprotected.
The big picture

When you see the word autoimmune, it is always pointing to this one central idea: the immune system has made a fundamental error — it is fighting the body it was designed to protect.

Everything described as "autoimmune" connects back to this breakdown in the immune system's ability to tell self from non-self, and the damage that results from that mistake.
